title: Founding of the IWW
body:
The Industrial Workers of the World was founded at a convention in Chicago in June 1905, where some 200 radicals, socialists, and trade unionists gathered to build what William "Big Bill" Haywood, opening the meeting, called the "Continental Congress of the working class." Among the founders were Haywood of the Western Federation of Miners, the Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs, the veteran anarchist and Haymarket widow Lucy Parsons, the labor agitator Mary "Mother" Jones, and Daniel De Leon of the Socialist Labor Party.

The new union rejected the craft-by-craft model of the American Federation of Labor, which organized skilled workers by trade and largely excluded the unskilled, immigrants, women, and Black workers. In their place the IWW proposed "One Big Union" of all workers, organized by industry, whose ultimate aim was not merely better contracts but the abolition of the wage system and workers’ control of production. Its preamble opened with the words, "The working class and the employing class have nothing in common."

title: Goldfield Organizing Drive
body:
In the Nevada gold-rush boomtown of Goldfield, the IWW built one of its first great western strongholds between 1906 and 1907. Working alongside the Western Federation of Miners, the Wobblies organized not only the miners but also the town’s clerks, dishwashers, and laborers into a single local, briefly winning some of the highest wages in the mining West and demonstrating the appeal of industry-wide organization.

The employers struck back through the Goldfield Mine Owners’ Association, which used a bank panic, wage cuts, and the pretext of disorder to break the union. At the operators’ request the governor secured federal troops in late 1907; with soldiers in the streets the mine owners imposed lower wages and blacklisted union members. Goldfield established the Wobblies as a serious force in the West — and previewed the alliance of employers and government power that would confront them for the next two decades.

title: McKees Rocks Strike
body:
The 1909 strike at the Pressed Steel Car Company in McKees Rocks, Pennsylvania, was one of the first IWW struggles to win national attention. Some 8,000 workers — many of them immigrants from a dozen countries, laboring under a brutal piece-rate and pay-withholding system — walked out in July 1909 against wage cuts and the company’s exploitative "pooling" scheme.

The strike was marked by extraordinary violence: the state constabulary, known to the strikers as the "Cossacks," clashed with workers in confrontations that left men dead on both sides. IWW organizers helped the polyglot workforce hold together across national lines, and after some six weeks the company conceded wage increases. The dramatic victory at McKees Rocks announced the IWW as a national force in mass-production industry.

title: Missoula Free Speech Fight
body:
In 1909, Missoula, Montana, became the site of one of the IWW’s earliest free-speech fights. When the city moved to suppress the Wobblies’ street-corner speaking — their principal means of reaching itinerant loggers and harvest hands — the union called on members to flood the town and defy the ban.

As IWW speakers mounted soapboxes one after another and were arrested, the jails filled and the cost of prosecuting and feeding the prisoners mounted. After roughly forty arrests, the authorities relented, and Wobblies resumed speaking and selling their newspapers on the streets. The young Elizabeth Gurley Flynn and her husband Jack Jones were among the organizers; the tactic pioneered at Missoula — deliberately filling the jails until repression became too costly — would define the free-speech fights that followed.

title: Spokane Free Speech Fight
body:
The Spokane free-speech fight of 1909–1910 was the classic IWW "fill the jails" campaign. The city had banned street-corner meetings to protect the "job sharks" — employment agencies that cheated migratory workers — from the Wobblies’ organizing. The IWW responded by summoning members from across the region to speak in defiance of the ordinance.

Hundreds were arrested and packed into overcrowded, brutal jails; several died from the conditions. Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, then only nineteen, became a central figure — arrested while addressing a crowd and later exposing the mistreatment of prisoners. The sheer numbers and the public scandal forced the city to back down, restore street-speaking rights, and revoke the licenses of the worst employment agencies. Spokane became the model for the free-speech fights that spread across the West.

title: Fresno Free Speech Fight
body:
The Fresno free-speech fight of 1910–1911 carried the IWW’s street-speaking campaign into California’s agricultural heartland, where the union was organizing migratory farm and construction laborers. When Fresno authorities denied the IWW a permit and began arresting its speakers, Wobblies from across the country answered the call to "fill the jails."

Jailed strikers endured beatings, freezing hosings, and a vigilante mob that burned the IWW’s tent encampment. But as more free-speech fighters arrived and the jails overflowed, the city gave way in 1911, conceding the right to speak. Fresno confirmed that the "fill the jails" tactic could defeat local repression, and it deepened the IWW’s presence among California’s farm workers.

title: Lawrence Textile Strike ("Bread and Roses")
body:
The 1912 strike in the textile city of Lawrence, Massachusetts, was the IWW’s most famous victory. When a new state law shortened the workweek and the mill owners responded by cutting pay, some 20,000 workers — mostly immigrant women and children speaking dozens of languages — walked out in the January cold. IWW organizers including Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, Joseph Ettor, and Arturo Giovannitti helped weld this diverse workforce into a disciplined movement.

The strikers’ tactic of sending their hungry children to sympathetic families in other cities drew national outrage when police clubbed women and children at the Lawrence train station. After more than two months, the mills conceded wage increases, overtime pay, and amnesty for the strikers. Remembered through the slogan "Bread and Roses" — dignity as well as wages — Lawrence stands as one of the great triumphs of American labor.

title: San Diego Free Speech Fight
body:
The San Diego free-speech fight of 1912 was among the most violent of the IWW’s campaigns. After the city banned speaking in a downtown "restricted district," Wobblies and their allies converged to defy the ordinance — and were met not only by police but by organized vigilantes.

Arrested men were beaten in jail, run out of town, and forced to run gauntlets; some were tortured, and the reformer Ben Reitman was abducted, beaten, and branded by vigilantes. Emma Goldman was driven from the city when she tried to lecture. The ferocity of the repression — carried out with the tacit approval of local authorities and the press — made San Diego a chilling precursor to the anti-IWW vigilantism that would erupt during World War I.

title: Paterson Silk Strike
body:
In 1913 the IWW led a massive strike of silk workers in Paterson, New Jersey, the center of American silk production. Workers struck first against the introduction of multiple-loom systems that threatened their jobs, and soon some 25,000 had walked out, demanding an eight-hour day and an end to the speed-up. The walkout effectively shut the industry down for months.

Organizers including Big Bill Haywood, Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, and Carlo Tresca sustained the strike through mass picketing in the face of thousands of arrests. In a novel bid for support, sympathizers staged the "Paterson Pageant" at Madison Square Garden, with strikers reenacting their struggle before a New York audience. Despite this solidarity, the strike was ultimately broken when the mill owners outlasted the workers’ resources — a costly defeat that tested the IWW’s ability to win long industrial battles in the East.

title: Wheatland Hop Riot
body:
On August 3, 1913, a protest by farm laborers at the Durst Ranch near Wheatland, California, erupted into deadly violence. Some 2,800 pickers — far more than there was work or sanitation for — had been lured to the hop fields by advertisements; living in filth and cheated on their pay, they organized under IWW members to demand better conditions.

When a sheriff’s posse arrived to arrest the strike leaders and a deputy fired a shot "to sober the crowd," a riot broke out that left four people dead, including the district attorney, a deputy, and two workers. State authorities blamed the IWW and prosecuted the organizers Blackie Ford and Herman Suhr for murder, convicting them on thin evidence. The Wheatland Hop Riot was one of the first great California farm-labor confrontations and a landmark IWW repression case.

title: Joe Hill's Trial and Execution
body:
Joe Hill, born Joel Hägglund in Sweden, was the IWW’s most beloved songwriter — author of "The Preacher and the Slave," "There Is Power in a Union," and "The Rebel Girl." In 1914 he was arrested in Salt Lake City and charged with the murder of a grocer and his son. The case against him was entirely circumstantial, and Hill refused to explain a gunshot wound he had received the same night, saying only that it involved a woman whose name he would not compromise.

Despite an international campaign for his release and appeals from the Swedish government and President Wilson, Hill was convicted and executed by firing squad on November 19, 1915. His final message — "Don’t waste any time mourning. Organize!" — and his reputed last word, "Fire!", made him a martyr. "I dreamed I saw Joe Hill last night," ran the song written in his memory; Joe Hill became the enduring symbol of the IWW’s struggle.

title: Everett Massacre
body:
The Everett Massacre — remembered by the Industrial Workers of the World as "Bloody Sunday" — was the deadliest labor confrontation in Pacific Northwest history. On November 5, 1916, some 250 Wobblies boarded the passenger steamer Verona in Seattle and sailed north to Everett, Washington, to assert their right to speak on the city’s streets in support of striking shingle weavers. Waiting for them at the city dock were Snohomish County sheriff Donald McRae and roughly 200 armed citizen deputies. When the boat drew in, gunfire erupted; in the space of about ten minutes at least five Wobblies and two deputies were killed and more than thirty people were wounded.

The clash grew out of a long, bitter free-speech fight. Everett’s shingle weavers had been on strike since the spring of 1916, and the IWW had come to the city to organize and to defend the right to soapbox on street corners — a right local authorities were determined to deny. Wobblies who traveled to Everett were repeatedly arrested, jailed, and run out of town. On October 30, 1916, a group of forty-one IWW members was seized, taken to Beverly Park on the edge of the city, and forced to run a gauntlet where deputies beat them with clubs and gun butts. The Sunday sailing of the Verona was the union’s answer to that violence.

As the Verona came alongside the Everett dock, Sheriff McRae called out that the Wobblies could not land. A shot rang out — each side blamed the other — and the deputies opened fire on the crowded steamer. Panicked passengers rushed to the far rail, listing the boat so severely that men were thrown into the frigid water; an unknown number drowned and were never recovered. Five Wobblies were confirmed dead: Felix Baran, Hugo Gerlot, Gustav Johnson, John Looney, and Abraham Rabinowitz. Deputies Jefferson Beard and Charles Curtis were also killed, most likely by the crossfire of their own side. Dozens more, on the boat and on the dock, were wounded.

When the Verona limped back to Seattle it was met by police, and 74 IWW members were arrested and charged with the first-degree murder of deputy Jefferson Beard. Thomas H. Tracy was selected to be tried first, in a closely watched trial in Seattle. On May 5, 1917, the jury acquitted him, and the charges against the remaining Everett defendants were dropped. The men who had been held for months in the Snohomish County jail were freed. The massacre became one of the defining martyrdom stories of the American labor movement — commemorated in Wobbly songs, pamphlets, and memory ever since.

title: Bisbee Deportation
body:
On July 12, 1917, in the copper-mining town of Bisbee, Arizona, one of the largest illegal mass deportations in American history was carried out against striking workers. The IWW’s Metal Mine Workers’ local had struck the Phelps Dodge copper mines for safer conditions, an end to discriminatory pay, and fairer work rules — vital war production that made the strike a national issue.

At dawn, a posse of some 2,000 armed vigilantes, deputized by the county sheriff and organized by Phelps Dodge, rounded up around 1,200 striking miners and sympathizers at gunpoint. They were herded into cattle and boxcars and hauled nearly 200 miles into the New Mexico desert, where they were abandoned without adequate food or water. No one was ever convicted for the deportation, which became a notorious example of corporate and state power crushing labor under the cover of wartime patriotism.

title: Pacific Northwest Lumber Strike
body:
In the summer of 1917, the IWW’s Lumber Workers’ Industrial Union led a massive strike across the logging camps and sawmills of Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Montana. Loggers labored ten- and twelve-hour days in dangerous camps with filthy bunkhouses; their central demand was the eight-hour day, along with clean bedding and better food.

With lumber essential to wartime production — especially spruce for aircraft — the strike drew a fierce response, including the army’s creation of the company-friendly Loyal Legion of Loggers and Lumbermen. Rather than continue a losing walkout, the Wobblies shifted to "striking on the job" — slowdowns and quitting at the eight-hour mark. The tactic worked: by 1918 the eight-hour day had become standard in the Northwest woods, one of the IWW’s most durable wartime achievements.

title: Federal Raids & Mass IWW Trials
body:
After the United States entered World War I, the federal government moved to destroy the IWW as a wartime threat. On September 5, 1917, Justice Department agents simultaneously raided IWW halls and offices across the country, seizing tons of literature, correspondence, and records and arresting the union’s leadership en masse under the new Espionage Act.

The prosecutions that followed were among the largest political trials in American history. In Chicago in 1918, 101 defendants — including Big Bill Haywood — were convicted in a single mass trial and given sentences of up to twenty years; further trials followed in Wichita and Sacramento. Hundreds of Wobblies were imprisoned, many at Leavenworth, and the IWW spoke of "2,000 class-war prisoners." The raids and trials, combined with vigilante violence and the postwar Red Scare, shattered the union’s strength.

title: Centralia Massacre
body:
On November 11, 1919 — the first anniversary of the Armistice — an American Legion contingent in a parade in Centralia, Washington, turned toward the local IWW hall, which the Wobblies had reason to believe would be raided and destroyed as an earlier hall had been. As the marchers rushed the hall, gunfire broke out, leaving several Legionnaires dead and the IWW members charged with murder.

In the aftermath, the Wobbly and war veteran Wesley Everest was seized from jail by a mob, mutilated, and lynched from a railroad bridge; no one was ever charged with his killing. Eight IWW members were convicted of second-degree murder and sent to the Washington State Penitentiary in a trial widely condemned as unjust. The Centralia Massacre and its lynching became a symbol of the violent repression that broke the IWW in the postwar years.
